chapter_theme: Medicine as a matter of measure. Illness comes from imbalance, the best remedy is eating with judgment so that no remedy is needed, and when illness does come, healing depends on careful diagnosis and on a whole system of people.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: what causes disease (941), food and its measure, time and fruits (942-945), lapses (946-947), the physician's cure (948-949), and the four parts of treatment (950). Most of a chapter titled 'medicine' argues for not needing it. Manakkudavar's text closes a section (துன்பவியல்) at 947, so his arrangement may differ from the received one.

941.reading: The three counted by the learned, starting with wind, cause disease whether they exceed or fall short.
941.nuance: Deficiency is as dangerous as excess. The verse defers to the நூலோர் and doesn't claim the theory as its own.

positions.position: What exceeds or falls short is food and activity, relative to one's constitution, and that disturbs the three.
positions.quote: உணவும் செயல்களும் ஒருவன் பகுதிக்கு ஒத்த அளவின் அன்றி

positions.position: What exceeds or falls short is food, sleep and sexual union.
positions.quote: உணவும் உறக்கமும் இணைவிழைச்சும் தன்னுடம்பின் அளவிற்கு மிகினும் குறையினும்

positions.position: What exceeds or falls short is the three humours themselves.

942.reading: No medicine is called for by the body if one eats only after attending to the digestion of what was eaten.
942.nuance: போற்றி, 'with care', turns digestion into something to watch. Parimelazhagar lists bodily signs of it, such as lightness and clean belching. His remark on உணின் concedes that this is hard to do.

943.reading: When digestion is complete, eat knowing the measure: that is how one who has gained a body can carry it far.
943.nuance: உடம்பு பெற்றான், 'one who has received a body', treats the body as a gift. Parimelazhagar pushes further: a human body is the only vehicle for this world, the next and liberation, so length of life serves those ends. The verse itself states no such purpose.

944.reading: Knowing the food is digested, hold to what is not incompatible and eat it after real hunger.
944.nuance: Parimelazhagar sets out three kinds of incompatibility: with one's constitution, with the season and hour, and between foods. His example is honey and ghee in equal amounts turning to poison, which Manakkudavar shares.

945.reading: If one eats with மறுத்து food that has no incompatibility, life takes no injury.
945.nuance: I'm unsure of Manakkudavar's sense. His gloss, with its example of ginger after jackfruit, doesn't obviously fit the verse, and I record it without claiming to understand it fully.

positions.position: மறுத்து means refusing the amount the heart wants and stopping at what brings no disease.
positions.quote: தன் உள்ளம் வேண்டிய அளவினான் அன்றிப் பிணிவாரா அளவினால்

positions.position: He takes it as eating by setting aside the food, with incompatibility illustrated by a compensating food.
positions.quote: சுவையும் வீரியமும் மாறுபாடில்லாத உணவை நீக்கி யுண்ப னாயின்

946.reading: As joy stays with the one who eats knowing how to stop short, disease stays with the one who eats enormously.
946.nuance: இரையான், 'feeder', is a word for animals' feed. Parimelazhagar notes that this likens the glutton to a beast. The contrast is inbam and noy, not health and disease: moderation yields pleasure, so restraint isn't presented as a sacrifice.

947.reading: If one eats hugely, not discerning the measure of the fire within, disease will arise beyond all measure.
947.nuance: அளவு occurs on both sides: disregard the measure of the fire, and disease loses its measure. Manakkudavar and Kalaignar read தீ simply as hunger, while Parimelazhagar reads it as the belly's fire.

948.reading: Investigate the disease, then its root, then the means that subdue it, and act so as to get it right.
948.nuance: நாடி recurs three times and sets the order: identify, trace, select, then act. Kalaignar adds that this applies to the diseases of society, which is his extension. Parimelazhagar lists surgery and cautery among the means.

949.reading: The learned one should act having considered the measure of the patient, the measure of the illness and the time.
949.nuance: Learning alone isn't enough: the verse makes the patient's measure come first, so that treatment is individual. Parimelazhagar explicitly wants both the book's way and the physician's own discernment.

950.reading: The patient, the healer, the medicine and the one who attends: medicine has these four parts.
950.nuance: The verse calls the whole arrangement மருந்து, so the patient is himself part of the medicine, not its recipient.

positions.position: உழைச்செல்வான் is the compounder, and each of the four has four sub-qualities of its own.
உழைச்செல்வான் is one who stands by to help, and treatment simply has four parts.

links.note: 943 teaches how to carry the body far. 968 asks whether keeping the flesh alive is 'medicine' when dignity has been destroyed. The health chapter treats long life as the aim, and the honour chapter, two away, makes it conditional.
The verses value the same body differently. 943's man has received a body and should carry it far, and 345's renouncer finds it one attachment too many.

A physician and a ruler think in the same form: 949 weighs patient, illness and time before acting, and 471 weighs the deed, oneself, the opponent and allies. Both end in the same verb of action (செயல்), and both reject a universal prescription.

Both use fire for the belly. 947's fire is a measure to observe, and 227's is the disease of hunger that won't touch one who shares food. One is the eater's problem and the other's cure is ethical, which widens what 'not falling ill' means.

950 divides medicine into four roles. 1102 says that other illnesses have other remedies, but the bejewelled woman is herself the remedy for the illness she causes, which collapses the roles of 950 into one.

source_issues: 943, 946: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
947: Manakkudavar's text ends with a section colophon, துன்பவியல் முற்றிற்று.
941: Pope's gloss adds food and work from Parimelazhagar, and turns the three into flatulence, biliousness and phlegm, which the verse doesn't name beyond வளி.
